Among retailers that started charging, 37% lost customers, 34% saw average order value fall, and 24% saw sales decline. The return is where a shopper decides whether to buy from you again, so a blunt fee shows up later as lost repeat purchase, not just a smaller refund. There is a version of returns that protects margin AND shopper loyalty by making the experience intelligent rather than expensive. When reverse-logistics costs went up, most retailers reached for the lever closest at hand: charge for returns. In 2025, 72% of retailers charged a fee on at least some returns, up from 66% the year before. On a margin model, the move looks clean. The cost of processing a return is real, and passing some of it back to the shopper reads as basic discipline. Then the second-order numbers arrive. Among the retailers that began charging, 37% lost customers, 34% saw average order value fall, and 24% saw sales decline . The fee did what it was designed to do at the unit level and undercut the very thing your acquisition budget exists to build. That’s the trap: you booked a cost savings, but what you actually spent was customer goodwill. Get The Return on Returns Learn the five-dimension framework, the business case for the growth and finance sides of your organization, and the metrics that tell you whether returns are working. Get the ebook . The return is when a shopper decides if they come back Shoppers don't file returns under "logistics." A return is the one moment where they find out what your brand is actually like when the purchase didn't go to plan. The checkout promise, the tracking, the on-time arrival: those were the easy parts to get right. The return is the test, and the shopper is grading it against a single question: if this happens again, do I want to deal with it? That is why the fee cuts deeper than its dollar value. Return experience quality is one of the strongest predictors of whether a shopper buys again, and shoppers do not separate "the return was a hassle" from "I'd rather not order from them next time." When you meet a return with a surprise charge and a slower, more restrictive path, you are answering that question for them. The cost you saved on the return shows up a quarter later as a repeat purchase that never happened. And repeat purchase is the cheapest revenue you have. A return fee is booked as a cost decision. Shoppers experience it as a loyalty decision. The bill comes due in the next purchase cycle, not this one. Two-thirds of retailers now name returns as a serious threat to profitability. They're right that returns are a margin problem. The mistake is assuming the only tool for a margin problem is a price. The retailers pulling ahead are treating the return as the moment shoppers re-underwrite the brand, and they're protecting margin somewhere other than the shopper's wallet. Four ways to protect margin without charging your best customers A flat return fee treats every shopper the same: the loyal repeat buyer returning one wrong size pays the same penalty as the serial abuser. That's the real inefficiency. Here are four moves that recover margin from where it actually leaks. 1. Aim controls at the abuse, not at everyone. More than 90% of return fraud and abuse comes from less than 3% of shoppers. A blanket fee is friction applied to the 97% who drive your growth in order to discourage the 3% who don't. Segmenting the experience — a streamlined path for trusted shoppers, tighter validation for high-risk patterns — puts the control where the loss concentrates and takes the penalty off the customers you want to keep. A blanket fee is friction applied to the 97% of shoppers who drive your growth in order to discourage the 3% who don’t. 2. Steer toward exchange or store credit before you default to a refund. A large share of returns come from fit, size, or timing, not real dissatisfaction. When the first option a shopper sees is an exchange or store credit rather than cash back, you keep the demand instead of handing it back. Exchange and store-credit flows can retain up to 60% of return revenue that a straight refund exits permanently. The resolution method also shapes the next purchase: Shoppers refunded to a gift card repurchase at 14%, nearly triple the 5% rate of shoppers refunded to original payment. 3. Make the policy legible before the shopper buys. Return policy uncertainty is a documented cart-abandonment driver. When the terms are buried in a footer or worded one way at purchase and another at resolution, that ambiguity reads as risk at the highest-intent moment in the journey. Surfacing plain, accurate return terms up front removes a reason to hesitate, and does it without loosening a single rule. 4. Measure returns by repeat purchase, not cost per return. Cost per return is easy to track, which is exactly why it drives blunt decisions like a universal fee. Repeat purchase rate among shoppers who completed a return is the cleaner read on whether your returns experience is doing its job. Manage that number and the fee question usually answers itself. Exchange and store-credit flows can retain up to 60% of return revenue that a straight refund exits permanently. Why this needs a platform, not a policy memo Each of those moves is obvious in isolation and nearly impossible to run by hand at enterprise volume. You can't manually decide, transaction by transaction, which shopper gets a fast refund on carrier scan and which one needs a second look, or surface the right exchange offer in the moment a shopper hits Return. For example, Narvar Shield provides that decision layer. blogs.content: 10 takeaways from K:BOS 2026 Generated by Klaviyo AI K:BOS 2026 wrapped in Boston this week, headlined by Klaviyo going headless and opening its platform to Claude, ChatGPT, and any AI system a team already uses. Across 10 sessions, raw model access mattered less than the quality of a brand's customer data and how intentionally it's used. Results ranged from a 13x jump in AI-search orders to a loyalty program that recouped $56,000 a month by rewarding identity over discounts. Context beats the model: Klaviyo's platform updates argue that an agent is only useful when it understands a brand's own data, reaches that understanding anywhere it runs, and acts on it for every customer, not which model powers it. Agentic commerce is already reshaping discovery: Orders originating from AI search are up 13x year over year, and identification, not messaging, is now the real bottleneck to reaching customers. Ambition on agentic AI is outpacing the data to support it: 73% of merchants call agentic AI a top priority, but only 28% have an actionable, real-time view of the customer to build it on. Consolidation beats adding more tools: Marketing teams running campaigns across 25+ tools lose an estimated 25% to opportunity cost, and fewer tools, not more AI, is what teams say would help most. Community and identity outperform discounts: A loyalty program built on status and recognition instead of purchase totals made members 3.3x more likely to place a second order. Sign up Get a demo Show AI generated summary K:BOS 2026 wrapped in Boston this week after two days centered on how brands build lasting customer relationships. As AI models become standard across the market, competitive advantage now depends on customer data quality and system integration. Klaviyo anchored this message by going headless, allowing teams and agents to access live CRM data and run workflows directly inside Claude, ChatGPT, or custom software. Across every session, a consistent theme emerged. Real growth happens when companies unify their customer data and make intentional choices about how and when to act on it. Here's what stood out, session by session, and what's worth carrying into 2027. 1. Customer context beats the model Klaviyo co-CEO and co-founder Andrew Bialecki opened K:BOS by making the case that raw model intelligence matters far less than customer context. Klaviyo backed up that thesis with major platform updates , including Klaviyo Headless, a new SQL engine, an evolution of Marketing Analytics to Personalization , and upgrades to Composer and Customer Agent . Together, these updates allow systems like Claude or ChatGPT to read customer data and run workflows from wherever a team already works, without needing to log into Klaviyo's own interface. Bialecki noted that an agent is only useful when it can comprehend brand data, access that context anywhere it runs, and deliver personalized experiences to every customer. Takeaway: The market is dividing into systems that unite data, reach, and action, and tools that only offer disconnected pieces. That structural gap will separate useful software from simple novelty in 2027, as well as which approaches to AI produce real revenue and business outcomes. 2. Build the knowledge layer, buy the rest Publicis Sapient ’s Duke Marr shared a 5-layer framework for building a brand-specific AI agent that can handle sales, service, and advice across channels. He recommends buying the parts that are already standard across the industry (the experience, data, and commerce layers) and building the two that actually make a brand unique: The knowledge layer: Your specific product, policy, and brand content data. The orchestration layer: The reasoning rules and guardrails that guide how the agent acts. While retailers are eager to adopt agents, winning consumer trust comes down to providing the deep brand knowledge that generic tools lack. Takeaway: Closing the gap between retailer ambition and consumer trust starts with data accuracy. Focus your engineering effort on training agents to answer complex, brand-specific questions reliably before worrying about full checkout automation. Klaviyo is here to help, too. We’ve built transparency, choice, and experimentation into Composer and Customer Agent so you can leverage the pre-built agents, while training them to your specific brand. 3. Agentic commerce is reshaping how customers arrive Shopify reported that orders originating from AI search are up 13x year over year, AI-referred average order value is running 30% higher, and AI-driven traffic to Shopify stores overall is up 8x, with younger buyers leading adoption of AI shopping assistants. Because these buyer journeys frequently bypass traditional website landing pages, brands have to find new ways to collect customer preferences before a shopper ever reaches their site. Takeaway: Modern buyer journeys increasingly start off-site, before a brand's own website ever gets a chance to capture anything. Getting more out of the forms, quizzes, and sign-up moments already running matters more now than optimizing what happens after someone lands on the product page. 4. Marketing and service are becoming one continuous journey S&P Global used industry data to project how marketing and service will converge over the next 3 years in Agentic ambition: How marketing and service become one journey in an agentic world . The research found 73% of merchants rate deploying agentic AI a top priority, but only 28% have an actionable, real-time view of the customer to build it on. Takeaway: S&P Global said it plainly: "Ambition is close to universal. Architecture is not." Stop planning marketing and service as separate roadmaps. The brands ahead of this are already building one customer journey on one data foundation. Take a quick quiz to see where you land on the AI maturity curve. 5. You can’t personalize for a customer you can’t see Wunderkind , AMB Interactive , and Lake Pajamas tackled a problem most marketing programs don't talk about: over 95% of site traffic arrives anonymously, which means even the best-built Klaviyo flows only reach a fraction of the people already engaging with a brand. Lake Pajamas closed that gap and saw email revenue per send climb 38% year over year, with a smarter 24-hour abandonment cadence lifting cart conversion 168% over the old 5-day version. Takeaway: Solve identification first, since a better flow only helps once you know who it's reaching. Identity resolution feeds more recognized shoppers into the Klaviyo flows already running, no rebuild required. 6. Composer is finding revenue teams don’t know they’re leaving on the table Snake River Farms joined the Composer team to show how the tool surfaces hidden opportunities and prioritizes high-impact fixes automatically, rather than waiting for a marketer to go looking. Takeaway: Composer brings the data and the ideas. You bring the judgment to decide what to do with them. The biggest wins are often hiding in the gaps of the campaign you already have. And now, SQL is available in Composer, too. Need ideas on getting started with Composer? Check out our prompt library. 7. Community is beating discounts, again Nutrition Warehouse and Okendo shared how Nutrition Warehouse built a loyalty program around community and recognition rather than discount stacking, rewarding the workout, not just the checkout. When they swapped a 10% discount code in their welcome email for a free shaker and towel instead, they recouped an estimated $56,000 a month, and loyalty members are now 3.3x more likely to place a second order than non-members. Takeaway: The same lesson as last year is still true: a discount buys the order in front of you, but as the session put it, "status, access, and identity buy the next 3 years." Check what your loyalty program actually rewards. If it's only purchase totals, it's a discount program with better branding. 8. Fewer tools is the fix marketers actually want Forrester rese...

blogs.content: In March, I wrote that the agencies moving from campaign execution to owning CRM strategy, agent orchestration, and revenue outcomes would build something their clients couldn't work without. Six months on at K:BOS, partners are further along than that piece predicted, and the opportunity in front of them is even wider. That’s largely because of what we shipped this week. There were major announcements, and each one changes a different part of your job. What shipped, and what it changes for you Klaviyo Headless. More than 260 Klaviyo tools and capabilities are now callable directly from Claude, ChatGPT, or any AI system. Read, write, and go live the same way you would inside Klaviyo itself. Partners are already building their own solutions on top of Klaviyo that connect your strategy, data, and IP to the power of the platform. This opens that opportunity even more, and allows you to embed Klaviyo directly into your team's workflows, supercharging productivity. SQL support in Klaviyo Data Platform. One consistent definition of your data, shared by every agent and every person who asks. Ask a plain-language question, get the same precise answer every time, with the definition and the query that produced it visible. This is live in Composer today in Early Access, and it's the difference between an audit you can hand a client and one you have to caveat with, “AI made this.” Personalization, which you knew as Marketing Analytics. The personalization layer now decides who to reach, what to show them, when, and where. It does this for every send and every touchpoint, and includes incrementality reporting that measures the lift against a real holdout. Your retainer conversation changes shape with this update. It is less "we built the segments," more "we set the strategy and guardrails, and here's the proven lift." We believe that as clients look more for outcomes over execution, this helps you clearly prove the impact of your work. Customer Agent, everywhere. Customer Agent is now available in 100+ languages and includes automatic locale detection through Shopify Markets that produces the right catalog, pricing, and currency for each market. A single Customer Agent rollout for a client can now also be a global one. The work is getting bigger As agents absorb the execution work, the projects partners get hired for aren't going away. They’re simply changing, and getting more strategic. For example: Speeding up sales by 3x by generating bespoke audits through Composer. Customer Agent configuration and governance. Restaurant guest data unified across every channel, in a category we barely served two years ago. None of these were service categories twelve months ago, and all of them are blue sky territory for partners to step in and own. These service categories are also the work that gets you into enterprise rooms and keeps you there: data architecture, multi-region rollouts, agent orchestration, governance, and compliance. These contracts are with more sophisticated brands for longer engagement periods across more of the client's stack. That's where this ecosystem is heading, and it's where our investment goes, training and enablement first, so you're ready before the deal is on the table. Celebrating the partners at the forefront of this next chapter Everything above is an argument for where the future of the partner ecosystem is heading. These 24 partners are proof that it's already working right now. The K:Partners Awards program recognizes those building what that future looks like: sharper strategy, faster execution, and customer relationships that last. Congratulations to all of these partners paving the way. Global Leaders Global Partners of the Year: IM Digital and Domaine Excellence Across Markets Americas Partner of the Year: ECD Digital Strategy and Un/Common Americas Technology Partner of the Year: PostPilot EMEA Partner of the Year: Mailody EMEA Technology Partner of the Year: Nosto EMEA UKI Partner of the Year: Enchant Agency EMEA DACH Partner of the Year: More Conversions EMEA Benelux Partner of the Year: Mailmeisters EMEA Nordics Partner of the Year: Woolman EMEA France Partner of the Year: Axome EMEA Spain Partner of the Year: Webimpacto EMEA Italy Partner of the Year: Jakala APAC Partner of the Year: Andzen APAC Technology Partner of the Year: Clearer.io Hospitality Partner of the Year: Plein Air Hospitality Technology Partner of the Year: Thanx Rising Stars Rising Star Partner of the Year, Americas: Pilothouse Digital and Lilo Social Rising Star Partner of the Year, APAC: Dynamic Cycle and Growth Gurus Rising Star Technology Partner of the Year: Orita Rising Star Technology Partner of the Year, Hospitality: Bikky What’s ahead This year, we said the future would be autonomous, agentic, and built with partners. We’re delivering on that. Next year, that future for this market gets bigger in every direction, and so do the possibilities for your business’s growth. Four things we're continuing to invest in, to support our mutual growth: Platform. We shipped 200+ features this year and put roughly a fifth of revenue back into R&D, and we’re not slowing down. That's what it takes to turn a $68 billion marketing automation market into a $160 billion+ autonomous CRM market—a platform spanning marketing, service, data, and agents—and it’s ripe for our taking. International. One of our fastest-growing frontiers, and we're building the infrastructure to match it. Expanded teammates on the ground, working more closely with our global partner ecosystem, and new routes to market to help you meet your customers where they are. Enterprise. Many of the enterprise conversations we are having start with the same problem, a business looking to replace a legacy system because it can no longer keep up. Partners are central to how the largest, most sophisticated brands adopt Klaviyo. Our $1 million-plus ARR customers continue to outpace growth of the overall customer base, and the opportunity ahead is tremendous. Your differentiation. We’re launching AI Expert badging, expanded Academy certifications, and a Partner Demand Center built to keep pace with all of it—focused on supporting your development and your success. We’re only 1% done, and so happy you are on this journey with us. Eddie O'Brien Eddie O’Brien is a dynamic leader with a passion for driving growth and building high-impact partnerships. As Klaviyo’s SVP of Global Partnerships, he leverages decades of experience scaling businesses and leading global teams to enhance our ecosystem – inside and outside of Klaviyo – integrating our partners deeper across our business. Previously, Eddie led global sales and partnerships at Gong, driving its expansion in Revenue Intelligence. He also held executive roles at UiPath, Automation Anywhere, and Dropbox, where he accelerated partner ecosystems and commercial growth. Earlier in his career, he was CEO at Arvato Bertelsmann and spent 15 years at Microsoft in senior leadership roles, managing multi-billion-dollar P&Ls and global sales strategies. Originally from Ireland, Eddie now lives in the Bay Area with his wife and five sons. He is deeply passionate about inspiring others to grow their businesses and careers through dedication, diligence, and resilience, always bringing energy and enthusiasm to every challenge he undertakes.
